findings.title: Pin and verify the remote installer before execution
findings.whyItBreaks: This follows redirects and pipes mutable network content directly into `sh` during the image build. A compromised origin, DNS/proxy path, or changed installer can execute arbitrary code in the build environment and bake it into the resulting image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever bytes this mutable URL returns. A compromised server, DNS path, or changed installer can run arbitrary code during the build and alter the resulting image without a repository change.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remote installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build fetches whatever content example.com serves at build time and executes it as root. A compromised, changed, or intercepted installer can silently introduce arbitrary code into released images; -sL also suppresses useful failure diagnostics.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported function discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a key deliberately stored with an empty value, so they may treat missing configuration or data as valid.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this helper discards that signal and returns "", which is also a valid stored map value. Callers of the exported API cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key containing an empty string.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Ignoring Load's error maps a missing key to "", which is also a valid stored value. Any caller of this exported API is forced to treat absence as a real empty value and can no longer make the error-handling decision available through Load.

findings.title: Preserve completion before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send is moved into an untracked goroutine, so Run can return while results are still pending. A caller can therefore act on incomplete output or close the results channel after Run returns, causing a pending sender to panic with "send on closed channel". The base implementation did not return until every result had been sent.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run returns immediately. A caller that treats return as completion and closes results can cause the outstanding goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; consumers can also observe completion before all results are delivered.

findings.title: Wait for all result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after sending every result. The new goroutines continue after Run returns, so a caller can immediately close or discard the results channel and lose outputs (or panic from sends to a closed channel). Result ordering is also no longer preserved.

findings.title: Require administrator status to delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: A session with isAdmin=false and the same tenantId as the record now receives true, whereas the prior authorization policy required both administrator status and tenant membership. This lets ordinary tenant users delete records.

findings.title: Require admin status for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: A non-admin session from the record's tenant now returns true, so any tenant member can delete records. The prior policy required both tenant isolation and administrator status.

findings.title: Restore the admin requirement for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: A non-admin session with the same tenantId now passes canDeleteRecord and can delete another record in that tenant. The prior behavior required both administrator status and tenant ownership, so this is an authorization bypass.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid stored settings now produce defaults. updateFontSize then changes the default font size and calls save, overwriting the user's existing settings rather than surfacing the parse error and avoiding the write.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of saving defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid stored settings previously threw through updateFontSize, preventing save. They now become { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }; updateFontSize overwrites fontSize and persists that fallback, silently replacing the user's theme and erasing evidence of the invalid input.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of saving defaulted settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts malformed or partial persisted settings into a valid default Settings value. updateFontSize then treats that fallback as real data and calls save; for example, updating a stored {"theme":"dark"} now saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, silently discarding the user's theme. Previously parsing threw before save ran.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch
findings.whyItBreaks: When `branch` and `verified` resolve to different commits, `builtFrom` identifies the requested branch commit but `artifacts` are fetched from `verified`. Consumers receive a self-contradictory report and can publish or inspect artifacts from the wrong build.

findings.title: Use the requested branch commit for artifact lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: For a requested branch whose ref differs from "verified", the report sets builtFrom to the branch commit but returns artifacts from the verified commit. Consumers receive internally inconsistent report data and can attribute the wrong artifacts to the requested build.

findings.title: Keep report artifacts tied to the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch and verified resolve to different commits, the returned report claims builtFrom is the branch commit but returns artifacts from the verified commit. Consumers receive a self-contradictory report and can publish or display artifacts for the wrong build.

findings.title: Respect the positive limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries instead of at most `limit`. The in-repo caller passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9; its loop then writes every returned item, expanding the initially 20-slot output array and exposing unbounded results.

findings.title: Restore the limit when returning sorted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every entry. renderFeed passes 20, then writes every returned element into a 20-slot array; with 21 inputs, assignment at index 20 extends the array and the rendered feed has 21 entries.

findings.title: Preserve the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9, so inputs with more than 20 entries expand its initially 20-slot output array and return the full feed.

findings.title: Keep entry-count consistent with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry has stale=true, the new filter removes its data row but the unchanged header uses entries.length. Consumers of the generated manifest receive an entry-count larger than the number of entries present.

findings.title: Count only emitted entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry has stale=true, its row is removed but headerLines still receives entries.length. The generated manifest therefore declares more entries than it contains, causing consumers that validate or rely on # entry-count to see an invalid manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any input entry is stale, its row is omitted but the unchanged header still reports entries.length. Consumers that use # entry-count to validate or preallocate for the following rows receive a count larger than the actual manifest contents.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting FormatLegacyID is a source-incompatible public API change. Any consumer that currently calls ids.FormatLegacyID can no longer compile after upgrading, and the deleted test confirms the function's concrete legacy-format contract.

findings.title: Restore the public legacy-ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting exported ids.FormatLegacyID removes a public package API. Any downstream consumer that still formats persisted or interoperable LEG identifiers will fail to compile on upgrade; the removed test confirms the expected output contract was LEG plus a zero-padded 10-digit number.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy formatter for compatibility
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported Go package API. Consumers that previously import ids and call this function will fail to compile after upgrading to this revision; no replacement API or migration path is provided.

findings.title: Restore the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function in the base revision, but this change removes it entirely. Existing consumers importing shippingQuote from this module will fail to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore execute's string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a `string` return contract, but every invocation now throws `always fails`; consumers cannot obtain a result for any valid input.

findings.title: Return the transformed input instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input) API now throws "always fails" and cannot obtain the previously returned uppercase string, making the runner's only exported operation unusable.

findings.title: Restore execute's result instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every invocation of the exported execute(input): string function now throws "always fails". The previous implementation returned input.toUpperCase(), so all consumers lose the runner's only successful behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the active viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only" at line 25. The new role predicate rejects that same request before handle can reach its viewer branch, changing the supported read-only outcome to "rejected".

findings.title: Keep active viewers eligible for read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. This makes the existing viewer-specific "read-only" result at line 25 unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only route
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Before this change the same request reached line 25 and returned "read-only", making that established role-specific behavior unreachable.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; an order `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` previously returns `"saved"`, but the added `payment === "paid"` condition returns false and makes it `"blocked"`. Payment is a valid prerequisite for submission, not for saving an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Do not require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns false for every order with payment="missing". saveDraft uses this shared predicate and therefore returns "blocked" for an unpaid draft, even though saving a draft is independent of submitting a paid order.

findings.title: Limit payment gating to order submission
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; therefore `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` now returns `"blocked"` instead of saving the draft. Payment legitimately governs submission, not draft persistence.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel other than "stable", the returned Snapshot.commit is the channel head from line 13, but Snapshot.files is read from the unrelated stable head. Consumers that use commit to identify, verify, or reproduce the published file set receive an internally inconsistent snapshot.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from "stable", the returned Snapshot.commit identifies the requested channel's commit while Snapshot.files contains the stable commit's tree. Consumers can publish or inspect an internally inconsistent snapshot.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build("x", limit=3)` still returns 10 items because the body unconditionally assigns `max_count = 10`; the added parameter promises observable result capping but has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the requested build limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns 10 items because the body continues to use the unrelated hard-coded `max_count = 10`. The new parameter's name and public signature promise that it controls the result size, but it has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises that callers can control the output limit, but the implementation always assigns `max_count = 10` and returns ten items regardless of `limit`. This public API contract is unusable for any caller requesting a smaller or larger limit.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. charge then turns '-1' into -100 cents, so callers relying on the stated validation can produce a non-positive charge.

findings.title: Validate positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') and parse_positive_int('0') return valid integers even though the exported name promises a positive result. Consumers can therefore pass a negative amount through charge(), producing a negative cent value rather than rejecting invalid input.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int(-1) returns -1 and parse_positive_int(0) returns 0, despite the public name promising a positive result. charge therefore accepts negative and zero amounts.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values copied df and returned the modified copy. It now writes through df.loc and returns the same object, so callers that retain df for later use silently observe transformed values in their original data.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values returned a modified copy and left df unchanged. It now writes through to the caller-owned DataFrame, so callers that retain df for later use observe unexpected overwritten value cells.

findings.title: Preserve caller DataFrame ownership
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values returned a modified copy and left df unchanged. It now overwrites df in place, so callers that retain the original DataFrame for later processing, comparison, or retry silently observe modified values.
